card.hook: It looks like a dark wooden wedding cake, with roofs stacked in steep little steps, and it has been standing on this exact spot since around 1130. You'll want to get all those layers in.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon, near Hopperstadvegen. The church is about 18 m away from it, to the north-east, so face north-east and you'll have it dead ahead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole church. If it won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved western portal and the roof tiers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up a vertical wall or corner with one of them, so the old timbers don't lean in your picture.
card.best_time: Soft, even light is best for dark wood and carving, so go for early morning, late afternoon or a bright overcast day. Midday sun can leave harsh shadows under the roof edges.
card.selfie_here: Try the far corner of the walled churchyard, next to the ticket kiosk. It's the spot one visitor rated as the best view of the church, so it's a good bet for fitting the church behind you, though that's a best guess. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the stepped roofs over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the churchyard entrance, with the church in view and the path leading into the frame, and you pose on that path.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed inside the church, and you may not be able to photograph indoors at all, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Get the whole stepped roofline in one shot, then walk up close and fill the frame with just the carved portal. Which one looks older?
card.good_to_know: Hopperstad is one of the oldest stave churches still standing in Norway. It was an election church in 1814 and left unused after 1877. The Society for the Preservation of Ancient Norwegian Monuments bought it in 1880, and between 1884 and 1891 the architect Peter Andreas Blix rebuilt the apse, corridors and roof, using Borgund Stave Church as his model.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon, near Hopperstadvegen. The church is about 18 m away from it, to the north-east, so face north-east and you'll have it dead ahead.

selfie_research.notes: No page names a selfie spot with the church behind the visitor; the cemetery-corner tip is written for landscape photos, so treat it as a best guess. The entrance viewpoint is described for photographing the church, not for posing visitors, and that photohound page's information dates from 2019. Sources conflict on tripods: PhotoHound bans them inside, while Pixeo says a tripod will help in low light (no ban mentioned). No page gives a selfie-stick rule. The Vik Church visible in the entrance-view background is a different, later building, not the stave church.

card.hook: White walls, green hills, big sky: Vik Church is the kind of building that practically poses for you. It's a classic white wooden village church, and it fits in one frame without a fuss.
card.stand_here: Face the church and leave a little room on every side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the church and its setting. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the walls and roofline. Only use zoom 0.5x if you move much closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the walls keep their detail instead of turning flat white.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to white walls. A bright but cloudy day works well too, because there are no harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera and step back until the church sits over your shoulder. Try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole building, and tilt the phone slightly up so the roof makes it in too.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working parish church, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or visit during a service.
card.challenge: Line the roof up with a gridline so it's dead level, with a little sky above and a bit of foreground below.
card.good_to_know: Vik Church was built in 1877 to plans by the architect Haakon Thorsen, and it seats about 450 people. The older churches in nearby Hove and Hopperstad were too small and in poor condition, so the parishes merged and a royal decree in December 1875 ordered a new church. It was consecrated on 23 August 1877 and had a major renovation in 1961–1962.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Use the phone icon on the map to find the spot in Vikøyri, then stand where the whole church is in view with space around it. Face the church and leave a little room on every side.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with Vik Church (Vikøyri) behind the visitor, or a spot where a passer-by can photograph a visitor with the whole church in frame, so both lists are empty. Most 'Vik Church' results describe Víkurkirkja in Vík í Mýrdal, Iceland, a different church, and I excluded them. Vikøyri pages I did find: Wikipedia's Vik Church article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vik_Church) confirms the church is in Vikøyri, and Mapcarta (https://mapcarta.com/29409958) says it is about 1 km north of Hove Church. Photohound's Hopperstad Stave Church guide (https://www.photohound.co/spot/1001977) suggests shooting from near the churchyard entrance with Vik Church in the distant background, but that frames the stave church, not a visitor with Vik Church behind them, so I did not list it. A Sogn tour PDF (https://cruise-norway.no/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/Vik-1.pdf) mentions a view of Vik and the Sognefjord from the Storesvingen viewpoint, but no page says Vik Church is visible from it. No page gave rules on selfie sticks or tripods, or a safety point for this site. Checking on site, or searching in Norwegian for Vikøyri viewpoints, may turn up a spot.

card.hook: Grassy burial mounds on a terrace, with the village of Vik and the fjord spread out below them. It's a quiet scene, and you can see most of it before you even get close.
card.stand_here: Stand near Vangsvegen, at the phone icon about 100 m east of the subject, and face west. It's about a 2-minute walk to the mounds afterwards.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole scene in. Then try zoom 2x to bring the mounds closer. When you walk up to them, zoom 0.5x held low gives a more dramatic angle.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, then add a bit of foreground like a fence, a path edge or some grass for depth.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the low light is softer and gives more texture. Bright midday light is flatter and harsher. Since you're facing west, the sun may be in front of you late in the day, so tap the mounds to keep them clear.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the terrace edge at the mounds, turn so the mounds are behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more in. For a cosier shot, sit or stand in the shade of the big tree beside one of the mounds.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the old road (Gamlevegen) that runs between the mounds, while you stand among the mounds so they frame you on both sides.
card.rules_and_safety: Respect any signs or fences and stay on the paths. The Hovsåsen loop that passes the mounds is described as needing good fitness and sure-footedness, so only take it if you're up for it.
card.challenge: Get one picture where the mounds look like little green waves rolling toward the fjord, and put the tree in the corner for bonus points.
card.good_to_know: Moahaugane is a field of burial mounds in Vikøyri. The mounds sit along a terrace edge with a clear view over Vik, the stave church and the fjord. One mound is known for its large tree, which makes a nice shady spot to linger.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Vangsvegen, at the phone icon about 100 m east of the subject, and face west. It's about a 2-minute walk to the mounds afterwards.

selfie_research.notes: No page gave a precise photo position with the mounds directly behind the visitor; the selfie positions are my inference from the descriptions (terrace edge, tree by the mound, old road between mounds), so check on the ground. The supplied position (61.07555, 6.58269) is roughly 250 m east of the mound coordinates given by Mapcarta and Komoot (about 61.0761, 6.5792), so use the named spots rather than the raw coordinates. Kulturhistorisk leksikon places the mounds about 200 m south of the church. Komoot's Hovsåsen page gives conflicting durations (up to 2 hours vs up to 5 hours). No page stated selfie stick or tripod rules, so the rules list is empty.

card.hook: Picture a small grey stone church with a stout tower, sitting calmly beside the Arnafjord, an arm of the Sognefjord. It only seats about 35 people, but it looks wonderfully solid.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, near Hovevegen, and face the church. Step back as far as the ground allows so the tower and the roofline both fit.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole church. If you're too close to fit the tower and the rounded east end together, go to zoom 0.5x and keep the church in the middle of the frame. Then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the stonework or the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line a wall or the tower up with a vertical line, so the church doesn't lean.
card.best_time: An overcast day gives soft, even light that shows off the stone. On a clear day, early or late sun adds warmth and shadows to the walls.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold the phone a bit higher than your face. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want the church over your shoulder, then check the tower isn't cut off.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a protected historic building that is used only for special occasions. Check the official site before you go to see whether you can get inside.
card.challenge: Get the whole church in one shot with the walls perfectly straight, then take a close-up of the stone texture to prove how rough it is.
card.good_to_know: The church dates from around 1170 and seems to have been a private chapel for a wealthy man. It was built in stages: first the rounded chancel, then a small nave, then a tower. In the 1880s the architect Peter Andreas Blix restored it and built the present stone tower, and he's buried under the church floor.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, near Hovevegen, and face the church. Step back as far as the ground allows so the tower and the roofline both fit.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie spot, a photographer position, or a spot to shoot the church from. Results covered Hove Church's history, location and opening, plus photo galleries, but none named a viewpoint. Evendo's Hove Steinkyrkje guide says the setting around the church is photogenic, especially at sunset, but gives no named place to stand. Hove Church is described as lying south of Vikøyri between National Road 13 and Seljadalsvegen, on Hovevegen, which is a street name but not a photo spot. The given coordinates match the church's Wikidata coordinates, so the landmark is correctly identified. Rules and safety are empty because no page stated any.
